title: Senior's toolkit: auditing TLS and weak crypto
summary: Test which TLS versions and ciphers a server accepts, find weak algorithms in code, and check post-quantum readiness.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: auditing TLS and weak crypto
steps.body: Security reviews and pen-test reports land on engineers as tickets: "server accepts TLS 1.0", "MD5 in use", "what is our post-quantum plan?". These are the tools to check the claim yourself and prove the fix.

toolkit.what: Force one TLS version to see whether a server accepts it. OpenSSL 3 refuses TLS 1.0 and 1.1 itself at its default security level, so lower it when you test for them.
flags: test for TLS 1.1 (the client would otherwise refuse)
print just the protocol, cipher and peer
offer only the hybrid post-quantum key exchange (OpenSSL 3.5+)

toolkit.what: List every TLS version and cipher suite a server accepts, each graded A to F. Quick evidence for or against a scanner finding.
toolkit.when: only against hosts you own or are allowed to test

toolkit.what: A thorough TLS audit script: protocols, ciphers, certificate, known vulnerabilities, with a report you can attach to the ticket.
See which algorithms your OpenSSL build offers. OpenSSL 3.5 and later list ML-KEM and ML-DSA.

.NET 10 ships `MLKem`, `MLDsa` and `SlhDsa`, backed by the OS crypto library (OpenSSL 3.5+ or Windows CNG with PQC support). Check support before you depend on them. `MLKem` is a normal, supported type; in .NET 10 `MLDsa` and `SlhDsa` are still marked `[Experimental]` (warning SYSLIB5006).
flags: sender side: a secret plus what to send

toolkit.what: The .NET analyzers flag weak crypto at build time: CA5351 for broken algorithms (MD5, DES, RC2), CA5350 for weak ones (SHA-1, TripleDES). Raising them to errors stops new uses.
A fast first inventory of crypto in a codebase, for a crypto-agility or post-quantum review.

steps.prompt: A scanner reports that `legacy.example.com` accepts TLS 1.0. You check, and see this. Is the scanner wrong?
options: Not proven: OpenSSL 3 refuses TLS 1.0 on your side at its default security level; retry with `-cipher 'DEFAULT@SECLEVEL=0'` or use `nmap --script ssl-enum-ciphers`
Yes: the error proves the server rejects TLS 1.0
Yes: TLS 1.0 can no longer be negotiated by any software
No: the error means the server only speaks TLS 1.0
steps.explain: "no protocols available" is a client-side error: your OpenSSL would not even offer TLS 1.0. The server never got a say. Lower the client's security level, or use a tool built to enumerate, before you close the finding.

steps.prompt: Match each tool to the question it answers.
pairs: Which versions and cipher suites does this server accept?
Does this server speak TLS 1.3, and with which cipher?
Does my OpenSSL build have ML-KEM?
How do we stop anyone adding MD5 again?
Where does our code use weak algorithms today?

steps.prompt: Enumerate the TLS versions and ciphers of `shop.example.com` on port 443.
steps.explain: `--script` runs an NSE script and `-p` chooses the ports. `-sV` is a real nmap option (version detection) but does not list ciphers.

steps.prompt: Sort the findings from a crypto inventory.
buckets: Fine today, on the post-quantum plan

steps.prompt: Your team can migrate one thing to post-quantum crypto this year. Which first, and why?
options: Key exchange (hybrid X25519 + ML-KEM in TLS), because traffic recorded today can be decrypted once a quantum computer exists
Code-signing signatures, because they are the oldest
AES-256, because Grover's algorithm breaks it
SHA-256 checksums, because they are everywhere
steps.explain: "Harvest now, decrypt later" makes confidentiality urgent: the attack works on recordings. A signature only has to resist forgery until it is checked, so signatures can follow. AES-256 and SHA-256 stay strong enough against known quantum attacks.

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: When a scanner or pen-test finding arrives, reproduce it with `nmap` or `openssl s_client` before you fix it, and run the same command after the fix as proof. Keep the weak-crypto analyzers as errors and a crypto inventory up to date, so the next algorithm change is a configuration change, not a rewrite.
